newsitem.title: UK: Mark slips on crosses as Buba stays silent on repo.
newsitem.headline: Mark slips on crosses as Buba stays silent on repo.

text.p: The mark edged lower against its crosses in European morning trade after the Bundesbank flouted market expectations and gave no word on its future money-market policies at its securities repurchase tender on Tuesday.

There had been talk that the German central bank could carry out a repo tender at a variable rate today as well as one at the fixed 3.0 percent as announced previously. There had also been speculation that it could announce the terms of next week's tender, perhaps with a variable rate.

Wariness that the authorities could take such steps to allow German market rates to rise had bolstered the mark on the crosses in early trade. But it shed these gains rapidly when the Bundesbank made no immediate comment on money market activities following the 0700 GMT tender.

"The mark was fairly firm earlier this morning because there had been expectations there might be a variable repo. But it turned out to be just a fixed-rate one, so the mark fell back on the assumption that German rates would stay low for now," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of forex at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The mark was at 978.70/00 lire at 0840 GMT, down from the 982.00 it was at just before the Bundesbank tender, and against 979.80 in late European trade on Monday.
Against the French franc, it was at 3.3734/35 against 3.3744/49 before the repo and 3.3733 on Monday.

"For now, people are selling off the marks they bought up on the speculation over today's repo tender and adjusting positions for the very short term regardless (of what might happen at the next tender)," Yamamoto said.
Analysts said the expectations that the Bundesbank might change its money market policy at today's tender had been overdone.

"That wasn't the implication from the Bundesbank meeting (of July 24). They had announced the terms for today's tender at that meeting so they would have had to revoke their own council decision if they wanted to change it today," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
The market was now looking to the next tender on August 12, with the mark's movements over the next week seen key.
A parallel repo -- conducting tenders at both variable and fixed rates -- is seen as a likely scenario, if not at the next tender then sometime in the near future.

"In the process of convergence for EMU...it looks like it might be difficult to make short-term rates converge at a lower level. So it's quite likely they will make this happen by letting German rates rise closer to those of other countries through a variable repo," BOT-Mitsubishi's Yamamoto said.

And if the Bundesbank did nothing after saying at its July 24 meeting that it was leaving the options open on repo rates for the latter half of its four-week summer break, it might dent the central bank's credibility and spark more mark selling, analysts said.
Meanwhile, the influential German Ifo economic institute's forecasts for 1997 and 1998 contained no surprises.

It said Germany's budget deficit would be 3.3 percent of GDP in 1997, above the three-percent target set for qualification in European monetary union, although it forecast the deficit would drop to 2.6 percent next year. It also said the Maastricht Treaty did not require nations to meet the three-percent goal exactly.
Ifo said its 1997 and 1998 forecasts were based on the assumption of dollar/mark being between 1.80 and 1.90 until the end of 1998.

It also said a dollar/mark rate of above 1.90 might "set alarm bells ringing" at the Bundesbank and make the central bank take "small steps" to send a signal to the markets. The dollar was continuing to strengthen against the German unit this morning, hitting its highest in nearly eight years at 1.8781.
German GDP should rise by an average 2.25 percent in 1997 and 2.5-3.0 percent in 1998, the institute said.
